title: the oldest hello
hook: you've said it after yoga class; the words inside say more than hello
carry: the light in me sees the light in you

segments.voice: You've said it at the end of a yoga class, and you've probably heard it means the light in me sees the light in you. The word itself says something much simpler. The longer meaning is a reading of it, and that reading comes from somewhere specific. First, a guess.

Namaste is Sanskrit, and it splits in two. Namas: a bow. Te: to you. Word for word, I bow to you. That's the whole dictionary meaning. So where does the light come from? From a reading of the word. The Chandogya Upanishad, one of the oldest Hindu texts, describes a light that shines above the heavens, above everything, and then says that same light is the light inside a person. Out there and in here: one light. Put that next to a bow and you get the popular line: the light in me sees the light in you. Not a translation. An interpretation, with a real source behind it. What the reading changes is who you're bowing to. Not someone's job, mood or résumé, but whatever in them is the same as what's in you. And nobody has to earn it first. In this reading, it's already there.

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Palms together if you like, or just sit up straight. Breathe in. As you breathe out, tip your head slightly forward: the bow the word is named for. Nothing to feel, nothing to get right. Just the gesture, done once, on purpose.
Namaste. Word for word, I bow to you. Read deeper, the light in me sees the light in you. First word on your strand.

howItsDone: Hindus greet one another with namaste or namaskar, palms pressed together at the chest and the head slightly bowed. The same gesture is made to elders, to guests and before images of the gods.

story.title: you are that
story.text: A young man named Shvetaketu comes home after twelve years of study, sure he knows everything. His father, Uddalaka, hands him a lump of salt and says: drop it in water, and bring it back tomorrow. In the morning the salt is gone. Sip from the top, says the father. Salty. From the middle. Salty. From the bottom. Salty. It's there, though you can't see it, the father says. The finest thing in everything is like that, and it's in you too. You are that, Shvetaketu.
